title: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions
pub: Manufacturing & Service Operations Management, vol. 16, no. 3, pp. 346-364
author: Tunay I. Tunca · D. J. Wu · Fang (Vivian) Zhong

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source evaluates auction design for procuring legal services, not legal AI’s capabilities, selective deployment, verification or human–AI workflow redesign. Its evidence on procurement-driven cost and quality outcomes is too remote to establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Procurement auctions: New bidders discipline incumbent prices
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: entrant participation can discipline incumbent pricing even when entrants do not win, while entrant awards themselves may deliver no significant overall benefit after quality losses are considered. It also treats these effects as conditional on auction design and market characteristics.
qs: However, the uncertainty in the buyer’s ﬁnal award decision in an open-ended format makes it suboptimal for the incumbents to keep their prices high: they bid more aggressively than they would in a closed-ended auction to minimize the risk of losing to low-price nonincumbents.

That is, there is no signiﬁcant direct overall beneﬁt for the buyer from the nonincumbent suppliers, as the price beneﬁt they bring is negated overall (as measured by the Composite Score) by the loss in quality of service when they win the contracts.

kp.k: Historical evidence concerns procurement auctions, not artificial intelligence
kp.d: Tunca, Wu and Zhong's 2014 article combines an auction-theoretic model with evidence from GECF's first online legal-services auctions, conducted at the end of 2003 across 33 legal categories. It studies changes in buyer procurement and law-firm competition rather than AI. Winning suppliers would collectively handle 95% of GECF's legal work for two years from January 2004, potentially extended to a third year.
qs: The online bidding events for legal services in our data set were conducted by GE at the end of 2003.
There are 33 different “rooms” or legal categories that the preapproved law ﬁrms bid in our data set.
The winning suppliers will collectively handle 95% of GECF’s legal work for a two-year period starting in January 2004, which may be extended to a third year.

kp.k: Competitive hourly bidding retained discretionary, quality-sensitive supplier selection
kp.d: GECF replaced traditional negotiations with dynamic reverse auctions in which law firms bid hourly rates for predefined expertise levels. Multiple firms could win; the lowest price did not guarantee selection. Economic Score weighted Bid Rank at 95% and Sourcing Rate at 5%; Legal Score weighted Expertise, Efficiency, and Capacity at 85% and Legal Rating at 15%. Their sum formed the announced Composite Score, but GE retained discretion to depart from it. This was competition over hourly rates, not a shift to fixed-fee billing.
qs: Suppliers are required to bid the hourly rates for predeﬁned expertise levels for their employees (e.g., associate, junior and senior partners, etc.).
Therefore, being the lowest bidder did not ensure being selected as a winner.

Although suppliers’ Composite Scores determine the ranking of the suppliers and help in selecting the winners, it is also important to note that the suppliers with lower Composite Scores are not guaranteed to be awarded the contract.

kp.k: Estimated savings came from incumbents and new suppliers
kp.d: The authors report average annual nominal savings of 4.1% against 2003 rates, with p = 0.08. Applying a 2.597% annual inflation adjustment, they estimate a three-year average cost reduction of 9.6%, or $17.91 million annually in 2003 dollars. Comparisons separately supported savings from incumbent and nonincumbent winners. Because future allocations of work were unspecified, the analysis used average winners' prices rather than observed expenditure shares.
qs: Comparing the nominal after auction winning hourly rates to the before auction 2003 rates, we ﬁnd that there is a 4.1% average annual savings, which is signiﬁcant with a p-value of 0.08.
The savings sum up to $17.91 million per year in total in 2003 dollars.
Since it is not possible to know the exact percentage shares beforehand, GECF uses the average of the winners’ prices as the estimate of the average winners’ price both before and after auctions.

kp.k: Measured supplier quality remained broadly stable as prices fell
kp.d: Quality analysis covered 31 rooms after excluding two without nonincumbent Legal Scores. Overall changes in quality scores were small and statistically insignificant, while Composite Score improved from 9.57 to 8.09. Winning incumbents had better average Legal Scores than the preauction incumbent pool, 2.98 versus 3.42 (p = 0.057); nonincumbent winners scored worse than the relevant preauction pool, 4.51 versus 3.51 (p = 0.048). Lower scores indicate better quality. These are comparisons of GE's supplier assessments: individual quality scores were held constant before and after auctions, rather than measuring subsequent service performance.
qs: Two of the 33 auctions in our data set do not have Legal Scores reported for the nonincumbents and are therefore removed from the analysis in this section.
Also note that each ﬁrm has a single quality score that does not change before or after auctions.
That is, conditional on winning the auction, average supplier quality increases for incumbents, which means that Hypothesis 2 is supported.

kp.k: New entrants indirectly pressured higher-quality incumbents
kp.d: The theoretical mechanism is not simply that more bidders lower prices. Under an open-ended award structure, uncertainty about the buyer's true quality preference induces high-quality incumbents to cut bids to reduce their risk of losing to cheaper entrants. Lower-quality incumbents are squeezed out, improving the quality of winning incumbents. Empirically, nonincumbent winners brought no statistically significant direct Composite Score improvement, whereas incumbent winners did. The model's conclusions depend on conditions concerning quality preferences and relative supplier costs.
qs: However, there are indirect beneﬁts from the inclusion of low-quality suppliers enabled by the auctions, as this causes higher-quality incumbent suppliers to lower their bids signiﬁcantly:
The highest quality incumbents hold on to winning spots, and lower-quality incumbents lose out.
Consequently, the average quality of winning incumbents increases.

kp.k: Quality controls eliminated statistically significant incumbency advantage
kp.d: In logit models using 198 observations, incumbency significantly predicted winning when quality was omitted: its coefficient was 1.051 (p = 0.007), equivalent to approximately three bid-rank places. Once quality-related scores entered, incumbency became statistically insignificant. Auction fixed-effects models and instrumental-variable probit analyses broadly supported this result. In the most decomposed instrumental-variable model, EEC narrowly missed significance (p = 0.108), while incumbency remained insignificant (p = 0.427). The authors interpret apparent incumbent advantage as potentially reflecting quality preference, not necessarily preferential treatment.
qs: incumbency seems to give an advantage to a supplier equivalent to about three places improvement in Bid Rank on average.
incumbency advantage is strong and signiﬁcant when the quality measurements are excluded but becomes insigniﬁcant when one takes quality measures into account.
Only in Model IV, the quality measure EEC barely misses being signiﬁcant (p-value is 0.108).
However, incumbency is again far from being signiﬁcant (p-value is 0.427).

kp.k: Actual selections weighted quality above the announced scoring rule
kp.d: GE announced equal weights for Economic and Legal Scores, but departures from that rule predominantly favored quality: 41 of 46 examined reversals across three supplier-pair groups favored quality over price. Estimated preference slopes did not differ significantly across incumbent, nonincumbent and mixed-pair groups. Pooling them yielded an observed mean slope of −0.69 and an inferred lower bound of 1.449 for the expected quality weight. Using the resulting revealed-preference score, the buyer's score improved from 10.95 to 10.13 (p = 0.017). These are inferred preferences, not a directly disclosed valuation.
qs: In other words, we do not ﬁnd evidence that the buyer violates the scoring rule more often when choosing incumbents over nonincumbents.
That is, the buyer in fact values improvements in supplier quality scores at least at a rate about 45% higher than implied by her stated preferences.
Rather, such reversals indicate a signiﬁcant deviation from her stated preferences in favor of service quality.

kp.k: Open-ended auctions offer conditional rather than universal advantages
kp.d: The model predicts that open-ended auctions can outperform commitment to a disclosed true scoring rule when buyer preferences for quality are sufficiently strong and supplier cost differences relatively low. The authors extend this recommendation to consulting, outsourced IT, marketing and selected differentiated products, while suggesting closed-ended auctions may suit generic, less critical products. The theoretical setting simplifies practice by assuming common knowledge of supplier quality and prices, and a single winner; the empirical evidence does not directly compare randomized open-ended and closed-ended formats.
qs: If the buyer’s preference for quality is strong enough, even in the worst case scenario
Further, we assume that each ﬁrm’s quality is common knowledge to each participant.
Again to keep the model simple, we assume that there is only one winner.

Simpler closed-ended auctions would more likely be desirable for more generic and less critical parts of a product for which quality may carry a relatively lower weight than cost savings and where the suppliers are relatively similar and none of them exhibits strong quality-based advantages over others.

kp.k: Long-term benefits require supplier diversity and quality monitoring
kp.d: The authors warn that concentrating awards among high-quality suppliers could eventually worsen prices, and that intensified price competition could damage service quality. They recommend maintaining supplier diversity and tracking historical quality scores through subsequent award processes. GE averaged 4.15 awards per auction, and 30.9% of winners were nonincumbents. Internal reviews in late 2004 and early 2005 reported buyer satisfaction, but bidders' private costs were not observed, preventing direct comparison of actual bids with cost-based equilibrium predictions.
qs: Increased supplier base concentration over time can lead to worse prices for the buyer.
Another concern with the auction process could be intensiﬁed price competition, which might hurt the quality of the service in the longer term.
Second, GE’s award process has multiple awards, with an average number of 4.15 contracts awarded per auction.
As is typical in procurement auctions, we do not directly observe bidders’ actual private costs.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no claims about AI. Tunca, Wu, and Zhong instead claim that open-ended online procurement auctions can reduce legal-service prices while maintaining assessed supplier quality, and that apparent incumbency advantages can reflect preferences for quality.
pts.d: The authors report that GECF's auctions generated savings from both incumbent and nonincumbent winners without a statistically significant change in overall assessed supplier quality. Their proposed mechanism is that adding lower-price nonincumbents, while keeping the buyer's actual quality-price preferences undisclosed, induces higher-quality incumbents to bid more aggressively and displaces lower-quality incumbents. They also find that incumbency ceases to be a statistically significant predictor of awards once quality measures are included. Award decisions indicate that the buyer values quality more strongly than its announced scoring rule suggests: their estimated lower bound gives quality-score improvements approximately 45% more weight than stated. These are claims about procurement design, not AI-driven legal-service transformation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims combine an auction-theoretic model with before-and-after price comparisons, buyer-assigned quality scores, winner-selection regressions, and revealed-preference analysis from GECF's legal procurement auctions.
pts.d: The dataset covers 33 legal-category auctions, including final bids, score components, winner identities, and incumbent hourly rates before the auctions. Quality comparisons use 31 rooms because two lack nonincumbent Legal Scores; the reported winner-selection regressions use 198 observations. The authors estimate 4.1% nominal average annual savings and a 9.6% three-year average cost reduction using a 2.597% inflation adjustment, corresponding to estimated annual savings of $17.91 million in 2003 dollars. Quality evidence concerns fixed, buyer-assigned assessments of suppliers and changes in the selected supplier mix, rather than newly measured post-award service performance. They report higher assessed quality among incumbent winners and lower assessed quality among nonincumbent winners relative to the preauction incumbent base, with no significant overall quality change. Regression checks include auction fixed effects and instrumental-variable probit models. Open-ended versus closed-ended performance comparisons are theoretically derived; the observed data concern the open-ended implementation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical claims concern auctions conducted at the end of 2003 for work beginning in January 2004; broader recommendations are conditional on strong quality preferences, relatively small supplier cost differences, and continuing supplier competition.
pts.d: Published in 2014, the study examines GECF's initial switch from traditional negotiated procurement to online bidding. The contracts covered two years starting in January 2004, with a possible third-year extension; savings calculations use a three-year horizon. The theory favors open-ended auctions when the buyer's preference for quality is sufficiently strong and suppliers' cost differences are relatively low. Its simplifying assumptions include common knowledge of supplier quality, one winner, and private supplier costs; actual GECF auctions concealed quality scores and selected multiple winners. Prices are final rather than subject to postauction negotiation. The authors identify supplier concentration and possible long-term quality deterioration as concerns, recommending supplier diversification and continued monitoring of historical quality scores. Their generalizations to other service and product markets are conditional recommendations rather than observed outcomes in those markets.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected parties are a large corporate legal-services buyer, its in-house counsel and procurement team, and incumbent and prospective outside law firms.
pts.d: For GECF, the authors claim lower procurement costs and improved estimated utility while preserving average assessed supplier quality. For incumbent law firms, stronger competition creates pressure to lower hourly-rate bids; higher-quality incumbents are more likely to retain awards than lower-quality incumbents. Nonincumbent law firms gain opportunities to enter the supplier base, and the authors argue that nonincumbency need not be a disadvantage after accounting for quality. The procurement mechanism still uses hourly rates by expertise level; the source does not claim a shift to AI delivery or alternative fee arrangements. The authors propose applicability beyond legal services to consulting, outsourced IT projects, marketing and advertising, and quality-sensitive manufactured products. They do not address access to justice, lawyer employment displacement, or changes in legal staffing structures.
